newsitem.title: USA: Astronaut's homecoming closer with shuttle's launch.
newsitem.headline: Astronaut's homecoming closer with shuttle's launch.

text.p: After six months in orbit, astronaut Shannon Lucid was one step closer to Earth on Monday as shuttle Atlantis roared into space to pick her up from Russia's Mir station.
The mysterious and unexpected shutdown of one of the shuttle's three auxiliary power units baffled NASA engineers, but flight controllers on Monday pressed ahead with plans to dock with Mir.
Atlantis lit the dark, pre-dawn sky with billowing smoke and brilliant light as it climbed away from its launch pad at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre at 4:54 a.m. EDT (0854 GMT).
"You can pass it along to the Mir that Atlantis is on her way," said shuttle commander Bill Readdy as the shuttle slipped into orbit 8.5 minutes later.
Accompanying Readdy aboard Atlantis were pilot Terry Wilcutt and mission specialists Tom Akers, Jay Apt, Carl Walz and John Blaha.

The sudden failure of the shuttle's auxiliary power unit, part of the shuttle's hydraulic system, prompted officials to consider bringing forward by one day the docking with Mir and ending the mission early.
Mission managers ruled out an early docking and were to meet on Tuesday to determine what impact, if any, the problem would have on the length of the planned 10-day flight.

"They will take a good look at all the data they can get on the (auxiliary power unit) and the circumstances of its operation," said Loren Shriver. "They'll also weigh the priorities of the mission and figure out what we want to do."
The auxiliary power unit is used during the shuttle's launch and landing to move its engines, wing flaps and rudder. The shuttle can land safely with just two operational units.
Atlantis remained on schedule to arrive at Mir late on Wednesday to pick up Lucid and drop off Blaha, her replacement.
When Lucid arrived at the Russian station in March she was slated to be relieved in early August, but a series of shuttle difficulties extended her flight by nearly seven weeks.
The shuttle's launch, originally scheduled for July 31, was postponed by six weeks because NASA ordered the replacement of its twin rocket boosters, fearing a dangerous flaw in the rocket's joints.

Menacing hurricanes lurking off the Florida coast forced NASA to haul the shuttle off its launch pad two times, delaying it a few more days. And a scheduling clash with an unmanned rocket caused a further delay.
The Mir station orbited high above the Kennedy Space Centre about 10 minutes after Atlantis' liftoff, providing a unique view of the shuttle's ascent.
"Hey, I saw the shuttle launch!" radioed an excited Lucid, adding some words of caution. "Just keep us informed because it's not here (yet)... I mean it's just a small step."

Atlantis will match the orbit of Mir over the next few days before Readdy gently eases the two craft together. A nudge from the shuttle's manoeuvring jets should dock Atlantis with Mir at around 11:17 p.m. EDT Wednesday (0317 GMT on Thursday).

Blaha, a former combat pilot and a veteran of four previous shuttle missions, will switch places with Lucid and spend four months aboard Mir. Blaha, 54, will be the second of six U.S. astronauts who will staff the station into 1998.
The shuttle is also carrying about 4,600 pounds (2,070 kg) of supplies and equipment for Mir and will return to Earth with 2,200 pounds (990 kg) of scientific samples and other gear from the station.
Atlantis is due home on Sept. 26, ending Lucid's 188 day stay in space, a record for a woman and the longest space flight by an American.
